THIS BOOK INCLUDES three separate parts. First, there is presented the "Discourse of Rome, " a tract by the French philosopher-psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan, bearing the specific title "The Function of Language in Psychoanalysis." Secondly, there are a number of notes written by the translator in the hope of explaining Lacan's very nearly incomprehensible prose. Thirdly, there is an extended exegesis of Lacan's thinking, written by the translator-annotator. In this section, Wilden seeks to introduce order into Lacan's writings for the general public not privileged to attend his seminars. It is of interest with reference to the field of psychoanalysis that Lacan is almost completely unknown to his American colleagues. In the opposite direction, Lacan goes out of his way to criticize American psychoanalysts as "philistines, " and to show his contempt for American preoccupation with experimental approaches to psychology.

The split in the psychoanalytic movement thus again demonstrated is, interestingly enough, so routine as to be one of the most repetitively demonstrable of aspects of that movement. The trend toward a narrow sectarianism, with repetitive dichotomizations within existing groups, has been seen repeatedly in the United States during the period in which psychoanalysis has shown remarkable growth.

[[RunningHead]]

Symbolization and the Sapir—Whorf Hypothesis

Edwin Weinstein M.D.

Edwin Weinstein

Edwin Weinstein  

THE CENTRAL IDEA of the Sapir—Whorf hypothesis is that language is not simply a device for reporting experience but to a significant degree, defines experience for its speakers. Probably the earliest statement came in an article published by Edward Sapir in 1929 in which he says

Human beings do not live in the objective world alone, nor alone in the world of social activity … but are very much at the mercy of the language which has become the medium of expression for that society. It is quite an illusion to imagine that one adjusts to reality essentially without the use of language and that language is just an incidental means of solving specific problems of communication … the real world is, to a large extent, built up on the language habits of the group … it is a self-contained creative symbolic organization which not only refers to experience … but actually defines experience by reason of its formal completeness and because our unconscious projection of its implicit expectations into the field of experience.

Sapir pointed out that there was no such thing as a primitive language (supposedly spoken by Freud's primal horde). Even the most primitive societies speak a language with a complex grammatical structure. Recent observations on the development of children's language have shown that by the time a child utters his first words he is able to classify them into subject and predicate. Here the grammatical structuring is an example of the integrative functions of the human brain and speech is as much of a biological process as walking. While a child may speak the most difficult of languages with idiomatic ease, he is quite unconscious of its lexical and syntactic rules.

[[RunningHead]]

Comments from the Floor11

Edwin Weinstein

Some of the earlier writings of Freud were very specific about language and the bivalence of language, with regard to what he believed was going on intrapsychically. Symbolism, specific symbolism, pictorial symbolism were really secondary elaborations. Language

1These comments have been edited for clarity and brevity. The identification of the speaker may be in error in some places.—Ed.135

was a representation of man.

I don't think Freud ever really addressed himself to the operational study of language. In his early writings, he referred to two classes of symbols: normal symbols and hysterical symbols. Normal symbols were simply symbols of which the speaker knew the meaning. Hysterical symbols were those of which the meaning was unconscious, e.g., an obsessive act or something like that. I think Freud accepted pretty much the findings of general philology. The main interest, then, was in the origin of the language—the ding-doing theory and the bow-wow theory, and also the theory that language evolved because there were certain interpersonal processes like love and sexual play. Acts weren't enough they needed some kind of embellishment. I also think Freud was trapped by arbitrariness. It used to be thought that the reason the infant said "ma" as his first word was because the sound engaged the muscles used in nursing. Then when they began to study primitive languages they found a lot of words for "ma" that didn't begin with "m." A tremendous change in psychoanalysis came at the time when after Freud's patient told him the story of her alleged seduction, Freud investigated and found it not true. If this situation came up today the analyst would immediately think, "What is there in the relationship between us that she is expressing in the past tense or what is the situation that she is using memory or an anecdote to represent?" Freud, obviously thought, "Well, if the incident hadn't happened when she was seven years, she must have had the wish then." I doubt very much if Freud ever took the communications of his patients from the standpoint of language per se.

DRS. LEWIS AND LANDIS have offered us a fertile paper whose frame of reference allows for the integration of various theoretic points of view, including the object-relational aspects of the more traditional Freudian approach, the object-relations theory of the English group, as well as the interpersonal point of view. This is made possible by organizing in a systematic way their observations around the concept of specific modes of relatedness that can be observed in an interpersonal field. It is refreshing to read the authors' development of the loose global notion of "symbiosis" into the differentiated modes of symbiotic relatedness, making possible an immediate application of our clinical experience to real, live relationships between people.

I would like to focus on one issue that is both explicit and implicit throughout their paper; that is the issue of individuation. Unfortunately scientific conceptions such as symbiosis and individuation quickly take on value-judgments of good and bad, of mature and immature. So it is that to be "individuated" is assumed to be more mature than "symbiotic." However to achieve a healthy symbiotic relationship is in itself a foundation to the rest of human development.

[[RunningHead]]

Growth and Change: The Patient's Experience and the Analyst's View

Albert Bryt M.D.

Albert Bryt

Albert Bryt  

THE PATIENT'S EXPERIENCE can be differentiated from the analyst's view. What is it that we are supposed to do for the patient, what is it that the patient wants us to do and what is it that we see ourselves doing for the patient? Finally, how can he test this? By and large the patient comes to us because he feels badly about life, about his life experience, and about himself. He does not know why he feels so nor how this has come to be. In other words, he's a stranger to the way in which he himself has organized his experience, his experience with significant persons throughout his life. Our goal in making this unconscious aspect conscious, in helping the patient view this somewhat more objectively, is to help him recognize first that he has organized his experiences which he often does not know. There has been organization. Secondly, we are to help him recognize how he has organized his particular experience. We refrain from telling him how he should organize his experience. I think this is often where we run into trouble. We forget that we can, at best, offer him some framework in which he can develop a multiplicity of options. As a patient he has only one option for living.

BURNHAM'S ARGUMENT is that a certain type of person, desperate for the support of others, will attempt to find personal significance in even very trivial incidents, eventually becoming a captive of the new meanings he has discerned. They may assume the power of superstitions over him, perhaps completely engross him, driving him into schizophrenia. Strindberg, says Dr. Burnham, never reached that final stage. He circumvented it by creating a kind of fictive world, identifying himself with figures of legend and myth. The result was a reborn sense of community, a reacceptance of dependence on others, and in that new frame of mind he was able to return to creative writing.

THE AUTHORS define the self-analytic task of the group on three levels: intrapsychic, interpersonal, and suprapersonal. The last being the "group-as-a-whole."

322

The leader's role is defined as leaders of the work group, "the work being to understand group process and structure." It may contribute to the clarity of our discussion to define these terms more precisely.

P.B. de Maré (1972) explored the theoretical background of groups and adopted as his guiding triad, the concepts of structure, process, and content. Structure, in his view, refers to the sociocultural framework, process to the communication network, and content to the meaning of what is communicated.

Hartman and Gibbard emphasize process and content but neglect the sociocultural structure in which their group operates. The word "structure" is used by them to describe intragroup phenomena.

Maré carefully defines structure as a sociological concept that "refers to the spatio-temporal matters of when and where and who, of the framework of selection, size, proximity, frequency, duration, etc. of for example small or large groups, primary or secondary, institutions, communities, societies, etc."

It is precisely that aspect of the total situation, its "structure, " that makes the group experience described by Hartman and Gibbard a mystifying experience for the students who participated in it. The fantasies of the group can be seen as resulting from what Laing describes as the struggle to make sense of the total life experience, in contrast with the reductionistic approaches of the instinct-based theories of Freudians and Kleinians, who emphasize part—object relationships to the exclusion of the total life situation of the patient.

The authors failed to establish a clear contract with the students and to approach the group from the different levels of its reality as a work group. There is first the level of the contract between the students and the school: what are the expectations of both school and students; how the course is integrated in the curriculum? They refer to previous successful experiences, particularly Bales at Harvard. However, from the material they selected it is also possible to speculate that the group anxieties are related to the self-contained, nonimpregnable nor impregnating nature of its members' experience. Thus, Norm, one of the students in the first group, sought to draw the lines of the group task, attempting to separate his intrapsychic conflicts by keeping them outside of the group.

Preconceptions in the Psychotherapy of Children

Maurice Green M.D.

Maurice Green

Maurice Green  

IT JUST HAPPENED TO ME this moment—something that sometimes happens to me with a child: I expect things to go along smoothly and for them not to give me any difficulty when suddenly I slip, and I say, "Oh, oh, something unusual is happening, " and then I find out what's happening inside me. So I found out something about myself now in relation to you as my audience, from catching hold of a change of tension and awkwardness in front of you. You just have to watch yourself wherever you are if you want to make use of these things. But since this is not a psychotherapy session, we shall not pursue this any further.

With the psychotherapy of children, just as with adults, we've spoken a great deal about its being an art and about its being also a science. I think that's what we carry with us—I think most of us agree to that—and yet we don't spell it out. That is to say, we don't precisely describe what is the scientific part and what is the art. In general I think that, at a minimum, science has to do with the regularities, prediction, outcome, and communication of reliable information. However, our aptitude, style, and craft—a unique, original product whether it be part of a tradition, like abstract expressionism, baroque, rococo, or whatever, or whether it be something outside tradition, like the works of Hieronymous Bosch—still have that quality of being unique and original in their articulation and form.

Comments and Criticisms

To the Editors:

Arthur Janov's primal therapy seems to be largely ignored by our practicing colleagues. One glance at the cover of his "Primal Scream, " which claims to be "the cure for neurosis, " seems to have been sufficient to put off most serious practitioners. They realize too well, after years of low-yield toil, that there are no panaceas in psychotherapy. Yet, among youth particularly, Janov is riding a powerful ground swell of admiration, as he provokes increasingly intense distrust among therapists of all persuasions.

It is conceivable that Janov has been beguiled by his own initial success just as Freud had been for several years when he adopted Breuer's "cathartic" therapy. He also believed then, that he and Breuer had a "cure for the hysterias." His increased disillusionment over psychoanalysis is now known historically. Indeed, his therapeutic despair (and perhaps, his cancer) led him to posit an intractable "death-instinct" as the basis for the "negative therapeutic reaction." Janov's patient acceptance and rejection policies may similarly contribute to his early successes just as Freud's patient-load of hysterics contributed to the success of his cathartic methods. Yet, the possibility exists that Janov's therapy may constitute an important contribution of wide-range applicability. His ideas and techniques would seem to deserve open-minded examination before they are derided and rejected.

Like Freud (and Sullivan, especially), Janov believes that the core of neurosis is to be sought in the earliest mother-child relationship. Like Ferenczi, Reich, and Perls, he emphasizes the patient's need for intensive experience instead of intellectual reeducation in therapy. Nor does he believe that dimly recalled experiences or the therapist's reconstructions of the past have much therapeutic efficiency. The patient's last experience, not the therapist's ideas, are required. Consequently, he encourages the patient towards a cathartic experience in which the raw, intense feelings that have been repressed in childhood, are derepressed and actively experienced at last. The "interpretation" and "construction" by the therapist is thus replaced by the intensity of an immediate instead of by a mediated experience.

To the Editors:

Dr. Ortmeyer's article on twin complementarity (This Journal, volume 6, No. 2) and the subsequent comments by Dr. Fox and Dr. Ortmeyer motivated me to test the theory of we-ego on a set of triplets which were hospitalized at that time for similar disorders.

The triplets were given two test series using a Rorschach Q-sort technique. This technique entails the patient responding to the card, then associating that response with one of three categories. In the first series given, the triplets responded to the categories mother, father, self. In the second series, the categories were the names of the three triplets.

There was an interesting consensus in the test associations.

WE ARE GATHERED here tonight to do honor to the memory of Harry Stack Sullivan. With his surpassing clinical and theoretical brilliance he was not always tolerant of slow-wittedness in his students. Students were known literally to tremble in anticipation of Dr. Sullivan. Perhaps this accounts in part for why I feel humble as well as grateful for your invitation to give this memorial lecture.

Sullivan was a great teacher. Not the least of his greatness was his gift for pungent and memorable phrases, memorable not just because they were vivid and attention-gripping, but, more importantly, because they captured, clarified, and provided organizing handles for even the most bewilderingly complex of clinical phenomena. One such phrase is "the extravasation of meaning." I have found this concept very helpful in organizing my thoughts about schizophrenia and have chosen it as a focus for the ideas I shall present to you this evening.

Edmund Braun  

I HAVE BECOME EXCITED to the point of being thrilled as I have engaged myself in the discussion of this paper, an extraordinary and beautiful piece of work.

Strindberg has reported in exquisite detail the process of consciousness that he was experiencing at the time of Inferno. Even more, he was able to report it with startling emphasis on the sequence of events and thoughts, the things that were happening to him at the time (in fact, as well as in his consciousness), and within limits, some of the feelings and "almost" emotions that he was having at the time they were occurring. Add to this the obvious literary talent in expressing this clearly and understandably, and in a form that invites one to "participate in the experience."

Dr. Burnham, in turn (in addition to his obvious literary talent), shows a precise and profound understanding of what Strindberg is talking about, beyond what Strindberg is saying. Dr. Burnham seems to have a very sure "feel" of the relative importance of things, of what goes into the making of what Strindberg relates of his thoughts and feelings.

One comes away with a feeling of Strindberg as a person, not, as I had previously thought of him (without much knowledge to go on), as a "black hole of depression, bitterness, and anger."

Paul L. Wachtel, Ph.D.
The City College The City University of New York

Paul Wachtel  

PSYCHOANALYTIC INQUIRY was dominated for a long time by a search for contents. Initially, hidden nuggets were sought and that which concealed them was regarded as merely an annoying barrier to the success of the analyst's depth probing. Increasingly over the past few decades, the organization of the ego has been recognized as an at least equally, if not more important determinant of how the patient has come to be in whatever dilemma brings him to therapy. Dr. Ortof's paper is an interesting contribution in this direction. She presents her patient's dreams to us not primarily to perform the traditional task of unmasking secret fears and strivings, but rather as an illustration of the patient's growing ability to reflect upon and organize the events of her inner and outer life. Dr. Ortof is not asking us to neglect the traditional lessons which dreams may teach us. She is, however, pointing to the dreams and associations to the dream, as a source of insight about the quality and organization of experience as well as a guide to content. This is a point of view all too uncommon in discussion of dreams. It is a viewpoint especially well suited to the communication of the experiences of another human being, as Shapiro and Schachtel have vividly demonstrated.

A note of caution is in order, however, about the use of illustrative excerpts from a richly detailed therapy process. Recent research has documented what we have all known all along, but have preferred to keep in the background—the ease with which one can derive impressions of trends in clinical material, whether they be there or not. The excerpts which Dr. Ortof presents to us do appear to arrange themselves neatly into a pattern of increasing ability on the part of the patient to reflect productively upon the meaning of her dreams and to conceptualize the events of her life. Our confidence in this pattern of progress would be greater, however, if we could be assured that the selection of excerpts was in fact representative of the kinds of dreams which appeared at different stages of the treatment.

Introduction

MOST SOCIETIES HAVE TO SOME extent delineated characteristic roles for the males and females to follow. Such role stereotypes serve as models for little girls and boys during their development, and their function is generally to ensure that the work and reproduction necessary for continuance of that culture are accomplished. Significance of Patient's Work in the Therapeutic Process

Francis Bartlett M.S.

Francis Bartlett

Francis Bartlett, M.S.W.
119 W. 87th St.
New York City, N.Y. 10025

Francis Bartlett  

MY THESIS IS that the patient's activity in the working alliance, just because it is work, is intrinsically antithetical to his neurosis, counterposes it from the beginning and increasingly becomes a source of change.

If the ability to work and to love are the principal aims of psychotherapy, they are also, in the form of the working alliance, the means by which the patient begins to move toward those ends. The changes which a patient has to make in his therapeutic activity, so as to work more and more closely with his therapist, are prototypic of the changes involved in his becoming a less neurotic person. The "alliance" has been extensively examined as a paradigm of human closeness, trust and intimacy. Its bearing upon neurotic and schizoid processes and its part in healing are now widely accepted (Kanzer and Blum; Sechehaye). It is work, as one example of the distinctively human mode of dealing with reality which I propose to examine here.

The aim of the patient's therapeutic work is to bring about some alteration in his personality and his mode of life. His work is rooted in the working alliance, but extends beyond it. His task, in collaboration with the therapist, is to try to find out what is the matter with him and the way he lives his life. He is responsible for revealing himself in the sessions as honestly as he can. As he becomes involved in the therapeutic process, he also becomes increasingly aware of the subtle complexities and consequences of his interactions with other people.

THE FOLLOWING REPORT is oriented to the discussion of a specific problem in genetic semiotics, i.e., how those states of human relatedness which effectively bind human beings into persisting groups emerge.2 The methodology of study is clearly "unscientific" in the ordinary sense of replicable experimental procedures. States of human relatedness which are most important in group formation are idiosyncratic, unique, non-replicable. It is quite impossible for the human being to fall in love, or to undergo salvation in any religious system, or to become illuminated or to experience the Aha-Erlebnis in a replicable or reversible fashion. Human relatedness is essentially irreversible and non-replicable.

This inexorable fact, put in formal terms in the metaphor of "time's arrow" used to refer to entropy, or in poetic metaphor in Omar Khayyam's statement that no number of tears will erase a single word of the history written by the "magic finger, " is that human life moves so that it cannot be revised. What happens later is always a superimposition, never a reformulation or a re-creation. For this reason, psychotherapy is a severely limited "therapeutic" method. It is not possible to reconstruct an unsatisfactory parental relation; one can instead only work to construct as useful a preceptorial relation as possible at a time which must (for many early processes) be inappropriate.

E. Rosenberg Ph.D. and G. Medini Ph.D.

G. Medini

G. Medini, Ph.D.

G. Medini  

IN A PREVIOUS PAPER (Rosenberg, 1971) some ideas were suggested about changes in the concept of experience. Among these was that the history of psychology, to the end of the 19th century, had been a gradual refinement of the analysis of individual behaviour. The psychophysiological techniques of Wundt, Brentano, Titchener, and others lay bare the increasing complexity and mechanisms of individual behaviour. Freud's thought was the great flowering of this historic line of analysis of the individual.

Beginning with the social and ego psychologists, the emphasis gradually changed from this vertical analysis of the individual to a horizontal interactional process, that is one person interacting and coexisting with another; where attention shifted from analysis of the individual to analysis of how the individual interacts with another person in a social situation. In other words, instead of looking at the person and his past developmentally and historically, there came into being an increasing emphasis on looking at a person horizontally, that is, at his immediate interpersonal experiences. Some of the words that belong to the individual are those that have to do with such concepts as developmental, motivational, ego. Some of the words that have to do with the horizontal, social interactional process, and it is a process, are sympathy, empathy, involvement, commitment, that is, interactional terms.

Individual analysis came at the apogee of a long and magnificent history of intellectual effort.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Psychoanalytic Intervention with Children

Stanley Spiegel Ph.D.

Stanley Spiegel

Stanley Spiegel  

MANY PATIENTS WE SEE have had previous experience in analysis or psychotherapy. Some of them have been treated as children before reaching adolescence. It is this population that I wish to talk about. When working with patients who have had prior experience in psychotherapy, it is important to know the details

166

of that experience, and in the course of treating adults we often note certain patterns in those who were analyzed as children which hamper their adult functioning. It is easy to say that this is the result of faulty child analysis. However, it is my contention that while the prior analysis may indeed have been deleterious, such effects are not the result of incompetence but the result of a basic theoretical error in the analysis of children.

In the development of psychoanalysis an attempt has been made to adhere to psychoanalytic theory in our work with children. Such theory is adaptable and useful in understanding children, but psychoanalysis as a treatment technique, as now practiced, is more clearly applicable to adults.

Experienced child psychoanalysts most often maintain the view that work with the child is essentially psychoanalysis as practiced with adults, and that to perform psychoanalysis with the child, one must alter technical devices rather than basic psychoanalytic method. One might ask at this point, "How many technical devices can we alter and still consider that the form of treatment is psychoanalysis?" There is a kind of quasiadherance to "the psychoanalytic method" which makes one apologize for modifications rather than accept them and fully comprehend their function and purpose. To adhere to the view that treatment should be the same as psychoanalysis with adults but adapted to children—a view I disagree with—the use of such devices as play materials, parent consultation, participation in activities with the child, all variations of basic psychoanalytic technique, are designed to interpret transference and to provide the youngster with insight. The language is adapted to the level of the child and interpretations made through play materials, although for some, the couch may also be used. Nevertheless, the attempt is to analyze transference and provide the child with an understanding of dynamics and etiology. I am not talking about poorly practiced analysis with children but about analysis conducted by competent child analysts.

[[RunningHead]]

Family Therapy as a Parameter of Individual Psychotherapy

Robert Counts M.D.

Robert Counts

Robert M. Counts, M.D.
103 E. 86th St.
New York, N.Y. 10028

Robert Counts  

AS WITH MANY RAPIDLY evolving treatment techniques, family therapy has come to be viewed by many of its advocates as a treatment method that is all encompassing, applicable to every patient that possesses an intact, or partially intact, family. A number of institutions have been established that provide only family therapy: services have also been established within larger institutions with the same intent. While this leads to refinement and elaboration of the tool it also leads to polarization. The "family therapy" agency or service often "feels" on the defensive vis-a-vis the larger professional community and is frequently attacked by detractors. The profamily therapy professional often becomes excessively enthusiastic about family therapy and de-emphasizes other techniques. A similar development of an opposite sort may take place with the "anti-family therapy" group. Pressures result in the "family therapy" agency almost becoming an organization cum dogma, and with a fierce parochialism not unlike some re-gious or quasireligious sects. Opponents are manufactured, if they do not exist, to serve as external scapegoats. This results in consolidation within the group, with internal discipline established and rigidly maintained. Criticism or questioning from within is viewed as heresy. Internal differences, reservations and cleavages are ignored and a false sense of conviction established. Later, these internal problems reach a point where they can no longer be glossed over and the organization perishes, or a new and more realistic appreciation of the agency and its treatment modality is reached.

DR. COUNTS PRESENTS a thesis based on three premises which would orient a clinician solely towards individual psychoanalytic therapy. He argues from the standpoint that there is a dichotomy between the intrapsychic and the interpersonal; that there is a dichotomy between individual psychotherapy and family therapy; and that individual therapy is somehow more profound, and consequently more valuable, than family therapy. We take issue with all these premises.

Sullivan pointed out that there is no way of observing what goes on inside a person's psyche. We can only observe what takes place operationally between the patient and ourselves as therapists, or between the subject person and significant others in his life. It is our belief that family (and other natural human systems) theory is the logical next step following Sullivanian interpersonal theory. Sullivan also emphasized the meaning to a person throughout his life of early interpersonal and heuristic developmental stages.

Miltiades Zaphiropoulos  

DR. COUNTS is neither polemical nor proselytizing. He leaves his points open to hopefully valid criticism and validly hopeful heeding. I will concentrate on psychoanalytic concerns about the subject matter.

I agree with Dr. Counts' reflections on the futile efforts and wasteful effects of a polarized dichotomy between family therapy and individual psychotherapy. The volume and the vehemence of recent literature notwithstanding, there is, indeed, much to be lost and little to be gained by defining the value of a "new" method or endeavor largely in terms of its exclusion or abandonment of an old one. Often this proves to be another instance of "the light that failed" for those who insist on realizing the illusion of absolute and everlasting incandescence, where reality requires persistence in the hard task of searching for enlightenment. The converse is true in the case of those who decide they have seen the light forever, no matter how dim the flicker and how continuously dark the corners. When the willful pursuit of the will-o'-the-wisp yields to the resourceful use of imaginativeness we happily run across an effort such as Dr. Counts'.

Fathers and Daughters: A Study of Three Poems

Mae Lord Ph.D. and Carole Stone Ph.D.

Carole Stone

Mae Maskit Lord, Ph.D.
Department of Psychology City College, C.U.N.Y.
New York City, N.Y.
Carole Stone, Ph.D.
Montclair State College
Upper Montclair, N.J.

Carole Stone  

MUCH HAS BEEN written about the role of the father in the development of his growing son, both in literature and in psychoanalytic theory. The theme of son searching for the lost father is familiar to us from the earliest works of Western literature, such as Homer's Odyssey to the reshaping of this motif in modern works, like Joyce's Ulysses. Freud's emphasis on the patriarchal influence gives us a father as identificatory model exemplifying conscience, character and purpose to his male offspring. The importance of the father to the growing girl has been stressed more recently in theory and research (Biller, 1970), (Chassequet-Smirgel, 1970), (Fisher, 1972), (Forrest, 1966), (Grunberger, 1970), (Spiegel, 1966). It is only now that we can begin to understand the role he plays in his daughter's development.

Therefore, it is exciting and revealing to discover that three contemporary women poets have written moving and complex poems that give insight into the father's significance to his growing daughter. In their poetry, experiences specifically feminine can resound and illuminate. Thus, we may follow Freud's well known counsel to those who wish to know more about femininity, and turn to poetry, women's poetry, for enlightenment (Freud, 1932).

The three highly articluate and talented women who have written these poems, Diane Wakoski, Sylvia Plath, and Anne Sexton, address images of absent fathers in tones of love, grief, and hatred.

Cognitive Changes in Psychotherapy: A Case Illustration

Edna Ortof Ph.D.

Edna Ortof

Edna Ortof, Ph.D.
20 West 74th Street
New York, New York 10023

Edna Ortof  

THIS PAPER IS CONCERNED with cognitive changes occurring in a 35 year old woman during the course of psychotherapy. The patient, a divorced woman with three children, came to treatment seeking relief from a long-standing depression, expecting to improve her relationships with her children and boyfriend. Like many patients, she hoped therapy would change her behavior and improve her emotional state. Implicit in this discussion, in which cognitive changes are emphasized, is the idea that changes in behavior and emotions cannot occur without cognitive modifications, since these play a major role in effecting such responses.

For the purposes of this paper cognition is defined as those processes which come into play somewhere between a stimulus and a formulated response. Emotions, like behavior, are at the response end of the continuum. These processes include attention and perception, attention being the selective aspect of perception. Before a response is produced, perceived stimuli are organized. This is done in a more or less concrete or abstract manner depending on the level of intellectual development and degree of psychological integration. Memory and judgment give added meaning to perceptions as these are understood in the light of past experiences and value systems. In a more general sense, cognition refers to any process by means of which one arrives at knowledge.

When evaluating patients' progress in therapy, clinicians tend to stay close to the response end of the continuum.1

Concepts of the Patient—Psychoanalytic Goals: Fact or Fantasy

Miltiades Zaphiropoulos M.D.

Miltiades Zaphiropoulos

Miltiades Zaphiropoulos  

THE PURPOSE OF of this presentation is to review: (1) some concepts of the theory and practice of psychoanalytic therapy; (2) certain preconceptions and conclusions pertaining to this; and (3) a few ensuing expatiations or expansions that lead to the consideration of psychoanalysis as a science and, eventually, to its contributions to a science of man. In the process I intend to be more critically exploratory than candidly expository, more subjectively selective than eclectically objective. This intention states from the outset that I have some serious questions regarding the relations between psychoanalytic goals as they pertain to psychoanalysis as a method of treatment, and psychoanalytic goals as they reflect scientific concerns or ambitions. My "questions" are neither new nor unique. But they beg to be restated because a number of proposed, proffered, or purported "answers" to them have tended to explain the substance of the questions away rather than to consider their ambiguity in depth, if not to accept their existence in perpetuity.

PSYCHOANALYTIC THOUGHT and scientific interest in dreaming have close, if not identical, historical roots. Within the past decade and a half, we have witnessed the discovery of a vast amount of new biological data concerning dreaming. As a consequence, a new "psychology of dreaming" is coming into being, with the evident need for theoretical accommodation, noted by even the most conservative writers.

There is much going on about us on the sociopolitical scene. Old values are challenged continuously. Confrontations occur wherever opportunity presents itself. A sense of transition, change, and flux has replaced a feeling of complacency and a sense of stability. Sociologists, taking note of this, are raising sharp questions concerning our institutions and the quality of life they evoke and foster. If the question of institutional change is on the agenda, as some of us hope it will be, then perhaps it is timely to consider whether a study of dream consciousness can contribute to our understanding of the reciprocal relationship between society and the individual. This, in effect, is to raise the question: Can there be a sociology of dreaming?

Roger Bastide (1966), a French social anthropologist, critical of the psychoanalyst's failure to come to grips with the dream in its social setting, does in fact raise this question. He notes:

D. W. Winnicott: Playing and Reality New York: Basic Books, 1971. 169 pages, $6.95.

D. W. Winnicott: Therapeutic Consultations in Child Psychiatry New York: Basic Books, 1971. 410 pages, $15.00.

PLAYING AND REALITY is a loosely connected collection of Dr. Winnicott's articles and lectures, which to varying degrees relate to the book's title. It begins with his now-classic paper on transitional phenomena and transitional objects. Detailed here is Winnicott's description of that intermediate area of experiencing in the child's development: the phase between the period when the infant's only reality is his inner one and the time when he can clearly differentiate the external world as distinct from himself. During this intermediate phase, phenomena may have characteristics of both levels of cognition. The transitional object, e.g., the teddy bear or blanket, although an external object is not fully recognized as such—so invested is it with internally derived projections of the mother image. Art and religion, as well as psychological illusory experiences, are other examples of transitional phenomena. They have their derivates in the transitional infantile stage and are composites of the objective and the subjective. The child who develops a symbiotic tie with his mother, is not likely to involve himself with transitional objects.

WE HOPE TO SHOW in this paper that certain fantasies of a bisexual nature observable in individuals have their counterpart in imaginative productions which serve important functions in the developmental processes of small groups. A bisexual fantasy shared on a group-wide basis may at times reduce the threat of hostile and competitive strivings within the group, enhance a sense of group symbiosis, and give expression to a desire for immortality at points when the group seems threatened with dissolution and death. Particular group members appear to play crucial roles in the dramatization of the bisexual dilemma. Of special interest is the member whose performance in the group can be described as "heroic." The hero more than any other member is inclined to act out all aspects of the dilemma as well as to portray a variety of possible "solutions" to both individual and collective conflicts. This paper represents an attempt to elucidate the inter-relationships among phenomena sampled from three levels: the intrapsychic (individual), the interpersonal, and the suprapersonal (group-as-a-whole).

It was Freud (1908) who first elaborated the unconscious bisexual significance of some hysterical symptoms.

IT BECAME A FUNDAMENTAL TENET of Melanie Klein's views on infantile development that the accomplishment of a satisfactory splitting-and-idealization of self and object was a primary requirement for healthy development. By means of this mechanism, in her view, it becomes possible for an idealized part of the infantile self to ally itself with an idealized object, in the first instance the mother's breast, as the bulwark against persecutory anxiety and confusion. The confusion particularly between good and bad in self and objects is, by this means, separated in a categorical way, exaggerated and rigid, it is true, but it affords a working basis for the task of gradual reintegration of the split-off aspects in the course of development, as the values of the paranoid—schizoid position are gradually replaced by those of the depressive position, with the relinquishment of egocentricity in favour of concern for the welfare of the loved objects of psychic and external reality. This gradual shift in values has a sweeping effect upon judgment and the estimation in which are held the various attributes of human nature. Thus goodness, beauty, strength, and generosity replace in esteem the initial enthrallment to size, power, success, and sensuality.

But the mode of operation of this primal mechanism of splitting-and-idealization has remained elusive and mysterious, the more so as we have become increasingly aware of the major part played by both inadequate and excessive use of it in the genesis of mental illness.

IN ANCIENT DAYS, the city of Thebes was afflicted by a monster called the Sphinx. Half lion and half woman, it sat at the main road and stopped all travelers, confronting them with a riddle. Only those who solved it could hope to pass safely. Until the arrival of a youth named Swollen-foot, all had been slain, but he was not deterred. He pondered for a moment when the Sphinx asked him "What animal is it that walks on four feet in the morning, on two at noon and on three in the evening?" Then Swollen-foot said, "It is man, who in childhood creeps, in adulthood walks erect, and in old age hobbles with a staff." At this the defeated monster hurled herself over a nearby cliff, for the young man indeed held the key to her question.

Many centuries later, Sigmund Freud again found a key to the riddle of man in the story of Swollen-foot, or Oedipus, as his name was said by the Greeks. In Freud's view, the key lay not in what Oedipus replied to the Sphinx but in the hero's own life. When Oedipus slew his natural father and later married his mother this interpretation has it that he was expressing sexual drives and rivalries inevitably at the core of his childhood relationships with his parents. The theory is well known, of course, to every reader of this journal. But not all would agree that Freud correctly solved the riddle.

UNLIKE THE EXPERIENCE of psychoanalysis in the United States, Freud came very late to France, and he was thoroughly attacked by Sartre in Being and Nothingness before he had even properly "arrived." Curiously enough, however, it was during the very heyday of existentialism and existential psychoanalysis in the 1950's and early 60's, that an unknown French analyst of Sartre's generation had begun a radical rereading of the Freudian texts. Reply to Professor Sprinchorn11

Donald Burnham M.D.

Donald Burnham

Donald Burnham  

I wonder if one reason for Professor Sprinchorn's objections to my paper might be that many critics and opponents have attempted to denigrate Strindberg's work by labeling him a madman and degenerate, to say nothing of bringing him to public trial on charges of blasphemy. Surely this is not my intent. I stand in awe and admiration of his genius and prodigious works. Nor, is it my intent to fit him into a preconceived mold. I believe that Professor Sprinchorn would agree that one of Strindberg's outstanding characteristics was that he could not fit or be fitted to any one mold. He was an enormously complex and divided man.

Strindberg, the anarchist, could speak of bombing the king, but he also spoke admiringly of Napoleon and Bismarck because they would bring order and unity. The realist was also a romantic, the atheist a providentialist, the scientist an occultist, the defiant rebel a humble penitent, and the inconoclast an inconophile. His hatred of society was in conflict with a hunger for social approval.

Psychoanalytic Theories and Images of Man—Structure of Psychoanalysis

Benjamin Wolstein Ph.D.

Benjamin Wolstein

Benjamin Wolstein  

THE APPROACH TO PSYCHOANALYSIS from the point of view of its structure is a comparatively recent development. During the past ten years or so, this approach has clarified a number of clinical and systematic questions.

127

Nearly all the questions I will raise this morning have been considered one way or another in our committee meetings during the past year, and in sharing them with you, I will attempt to suggest their relevance—with the hope that further discussion will extend and sharpen their relevance.

But first to sketch a structure of psychoanalysis comprising the essential features of its therapeutic inquiry. It has observations and definitions, postulates or points of view and theory, and finally, perspectives on metapsychology.

At the empirical level, the major observations to be made and defined are transference, resistance, anxiety and counteranxiety, counterresistance and countertransference.

At the systematic level, the major postulates or points of view to be applied to defined observations are genesis and function, structure and dynamism, immediacy and reflection, and the controlling theory of unconscious or dissociated experience.

At the interpretive level, the major metapsychologies are pluralistic and diverse, from those of Freud, Adler, Jung, and Rank, through Reich, Anna Freud and Hartmann, Kris, and Lowenstein, to Fromm, Horney, Sullivan, and Thompson, to the many, many more individual and less publicized ones now being used in actual practice. Generally, they all tend to fall into three main types—biological, sociological, psychological—but none, of course, represents a pure type.

To turn to the questions: First, what are the constituents and conditions of therapeutic experience that make psychoanalysis possible? What features are common to all psychoanalytic therapy? And how do they distinguish it from other psychotherapies?

Second, what is a psychoanalytic fact? as distinct from a biological fact? a sociological fact? or, even, a linguistic fact? From what inquiry do we derive it? And in what terms do we support it? How, in short, does analysis of transference and countertransference and so on, bring a particular patient and his particular psychoanalyst to the personal limits of their shared experience?

IN THE NAME OF the Committee on Psychoanalysis as a Science of Man, which expresses one of the Institute's concerns, welcome to today's all-day sessions. Members of this committee will present ideas that had some determination in our group discussion—questions and ideas raised by individuals and bounced back and forth in the group as sounding board. In addition to presenting these ideas we very much desire a response from the audience, a free and spontaneous response, and for that reason we are restricting the presentations by the panelists to ten minutes each in order to allow greater participation by the audience. What will be presented cannot possibly be complete because of time and because some of the subjects touch on such profound matters that there simply couldn't be closure.

The impetus for this committee, and so the impetus for today's meeting, comes from Earl Witenberg's concern and confrontation as to what the direction of an institute for psychoanalysis can be in the immediate future, say, in units of five, ten, fifteen years. Is the future of the White Institute to take shape as an institute for the science of man? This committee was given its mandate by the Board of Fellows to explore ideas, whatever they might be and from whatever source, that would be relevant to this concern and without any precharting of our course. We were given, so to speak, the opportunity for a confrontation with the unknown. The unknown was unknown in terms of method and in terms of content.

This committee is now in its fourth year. The first year considered what the philosophy of science might have to offer us starting in under the chairmanship of the first chairman, Rollo May, with a brilliant weekend seminar under Professor Abraham Kaplan.

Symbiotic Pairings in Adults

Alfred Lewis M.D. and Bernard Landis Ph.D.

Bernard Landis

Alfred B. Lewis, Jr., M.D.
Bernard Landis, Ph.D.
525 East 68 Street
New York, N.Y. 10021

Bernard Landis  

SUMMARY

It is our experience that the application of the biological concept of symbiosis to psychology provides a useful metaphor for understanding certain kinds of distorted human relatedness. The metaphor has been widely, but imprecisely, applied to pathologically intimate mother—child relationships. Sporadic attempts have also been made to apply it to other relationships which appear to have symbiotic characteristics. The purpose of this paper has been to clarify some of the resulting confusion. In the process, we have extended the concept of symbiosis to a much broader spectrum of human relationships and have identified and described several different kinds of symbiosis. We have found it useful to characterize relationships in which the original mother—child symbiosis has persisted into adulthood as "primary symbiosis, " and to group all other symbiotic patterns under the term "secondary symbiosis." The latter term embraces those relationships in which a stable symbiotic pattern is reconstituted with someone else than the mother ("Stable Secondary Symbiosis"), and relationships which are transitory and primarily imitative in character ("Floating Symbiosis"). It also embraces a pattern of behavior which we call "Negative Symbiosis" in which intimacy is avoided because it raises the fear of symbiotic regression. The need to escape a maternal presence perceived as engulfing, or the fear that intimacy will lead to symbiotic regression can be a powerful impetus to "acting out" behavior, especially in the sexual area; thus an understanding of negative symbiosis can be most helpful in clarifying the dynamic basis of acting out disorders.

Our formulation of the concept of symbiosis from the developmental, phenomenological, structural, and functional points of

247

view has led to some changes in emphasis from the more conventional psychopathological approaches. From the developmental viewpoint, it has led us to a heightened awareness of the vicissitudes of the individuation process, and the obstacles thereto. From the phenomenologic viewpoint it has led us to an increased emphasis on understanding the patient's experience of being alone, or conversely, his experience of intimacy with another person. From the structural viewpoint, greater emphasis must be placed on understanding the internalized representations of the self and of meaningful objects, and the integrity of the boundaries between those representations. And from the functional viewpoint, the emphasis must be on understanding the defensive function which the symbiotic relationship fulfills.

Harry Guntrip Ph.D.

Harry Guntrip  

IF I WERE ASKED to quote one passage that more than any other expresses the fundamental truth and problem about human nature, I would quote, not any passage from Freud, but one from Bertrand Russell. I must defer for the moment the citing of this passage since, to feel its full force, we must pave the way for it. Yet, in spite of the profundity of that one passage, Russell's life work has contributed little of permanent value for man, in a practical sense, while Freud started what has become the profoundest research into human nature ever yet made. The intriguing problem is why did Russell's profound insight lie sterile and unused in all his later work, while Freud's less profound early observations and tentative theories developed into a systematic "penetration" (to use Russell's own word) into that very region of human experience that Russell might have explored.

Freud and Russell, two of the intellectual giants of the end of last century and the first half of this one, may seem, at first sight, to be an unlikely pair to choose for a comparative study. They reveal, however, not only striking differences but also unexpectedly intriguing parallels. There is a superficial overall parallel in that both of them began with an apparently total dedication to impersonal intellectual work, the one in physical science, the other in philosophy, but in due course both of them moved on to become steeped, in different ways, in most practical human problems. If Freud's early interest was not quite so abstractly intellectual as was Russell's in geometry, his interest in human nature was more intellectual than practical.

Cannibalistic Tenderness in Nongenital Sensuality

M. Masud Khan

M. Masud Khan

M. Masud R. Khan
Flat 9
3 Hans Crescent
London SWIX OLN

M. Masud Khan  

Les philosophes ordinaires ont soumis l'homme a la nature pour s'accommoder aux idees recues: prenant un vol plus rapide, je te prouverai, quand tu voudras, qu'il n'en depend nullement.
de Sade

Introduction

FREUD, IN HIS "Three Essays on Sexuality" (1905), had given the whole concept of cannibalism a new dimension. He had discriminated cannibalistic features in infantile sexuality. Freud considered the cannibalistic desires of infantile sexuality intimately related to sadism and the aggressive factor in the libido. To the cannibalistic pregenital sexual organization Freud further attributed the aims of incorporation of the object and obtaining mastery over it.

Pursuing the route indicated by Freud, I shall offer a different significance of the cannibalistic features in adult human sexuality, be it in the foreplay preceding genital intercourse or in perversions proper, where it usurps unto itself an exclusive role and purpose. Following Freud, almost all analytic thinkers have placed too much emphasis on the sadistic and coercive nature of the cannibalistic impulses. I shall try to show that it has tender features as well, and serves functions other than those of incorporating and mastering the not-self object.

Ruth Moulton

Ruth Moulton  

MY COMMENTS on this paper are based on my supervisory work with Dr. Ortof as she struggled to get this difficult patient into a workable analytic relationship. The patient was originally accepted for treatment because she presented primarily her depression and deepseated need for personal help to the screeners. However, the beginning months of treatment were very discouraging. The depression lifted rather readily on a transference basis when she sensed the presence of a helping person. She then became preoccupied with external realities, the lack of a husband, the lack of money, the burden of raising her children alone and focused on her need for help with external problems. Especially, she seemed to want therapy to help her get married to her boyfriend. It was quite clear that she wanted her new and better mother to find a replacement for her absent dead father as seen in Dream A. In Dream B, actually the first one after she started analysis, she showed little hope for internal change. It is as though she would settle for a new facade, for superficial change, for better "make-up." After her father's death when she was 12, she experienced her mother as increasingly critical. External appearances were stressed by such degrading remarks as, "Put on some make-up, you look like you're dying." (a good background for Dream B.) Her ambivalence about treatment, her fears that a woman near her own age could not possibly satisfy her inordinate needs became clear as a second stage of regression occurred. She quit her job and for a short time could not pay even the low established fee. She found her dreams baffling and irrelevant, seemed unable to interpret them, showed little ability to use her dream images as symbols and seemed to have a restrictive way of thinking. It was hard to get her to look inside herself because the outside dilemas in her life seemed so pressing. Some of the catastrophes such as a fire in her apartment (which occurred before treatment) seemed partly related to her enormous resentment at having to carry so much responsibility without any other adult to help. The background for this cognitive constriction seemed to rest on an emotionally and culturally impoverished background. Feelings were overlooked by both parents.
